newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Elf reports profit jump, ambitions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Elf reports profit jump, ambitions.

text.p: France's Elf Aquitaine SA, the world's eighth largest oil group, reported a 41 percent rise in 1996 net profit on Wednesday, raised its dividend and set an ambitious plan to challenge its bigger rivals.
Elf's net income, before restructuring charges, rose to 7.52 billion francs ($1.3 billion) from 5.32 billion in 1995. Sales were 232.71 billion francs, up from 208.29 billion the previous year.
It raised its net dividend to 14 francs per share from 13 and profit per share rose to 28 francs from 20.
Elf shares closed 0.92 percent higher at 547 francs while French blue-chip index was down 0.21 percent.
The figures were in line with analysts' expectations because the company had already announced in December that net income would be between 7.3 and 7.5 billion francs.
"There was certainly a marked improvement in results from the production and exploration side," Salomon Brothers analyst Gordon Gray told Reuters Financial Television.
Operating income from exploration and production almost doubled to 15.49 billion francs in 1996 from 8.01 billion in 1995.
The overall profit represents a return on equity -- a key yardstick of profitability -- of 9.5 percent against 6.9 percent in 1995. But this was partly due to a good economic environment.
Chairman Philippe Jaffre said the company was aiming for a return of at least 10 percent in 1998, even with a less favourable economic climate, and it should rise to 12 percent later on.
This would put Elf on a level with oil majors like Exxon and Royal Dutch/Shell.
"Our numbers are indicating that they should be able to achieve that kind of return," Salomon's Gray said, adding he believed Elf remained one of the best stocks in the European energy sector.

Jaffre said only half of the 6.8 billion franc increase in operating income to 21.73 billion francs was due to improved economic conditions. Production growth accounted for 15 percent of the rise and increased efficiency 35 percent.
It took 541 million francs in restructuring charges, mainly for staff cuts through early retirement and voluntary departures.
"This improvement is not only due to high oil prices. Our course would not have been as satisfying if we had not developed our businesses while continuing to reduce our costs," he said.

"Our objective is to grow Elf's value for shareholders by transforming Elf from a European company into a leading international corporation with a level of profitability which is equal to the best," Jaffre added.
Elf did not make a forecast for 1997, saying this depended largely on crude oil prices, recent high levels of which were unlikely to be sustained.
But he said: "For 1997, I am rather optimistic," adding that the economy seemed to be growing sustainably, interest rates were low and European integration was close.
"Elf has raised itself to among the top 10 oil companies in the world, among the first 20 chemical groups of the world and among the 30 leading international drugs companies," he said.
"In 2005, Elf will be a world company with 40 percent of its activities in America, Asia and Africa. In all of its activities it will be among the top 10 in the respective sectors," he said.
In the year 2000, Elf aims to generate a third of its sales outside Europe, compared with a quarter now.

In refining, marketing and trading, operating income soared to 147 million francs from four million in 1995. In chemicals, operating income fell to 3.65 billion francs from 4.96 billion. In health, where Elf owns 55 percent of Sanofi, operating income slid to 2.46 billion francs from 2.49 billion. ($ = 5.640 French Francs)
